tur55-1: Spondylolisthesis is the forward slipping of one vertebra over the vertebra below it; it is most common at the two lowest levels of the lower back (L4–L5 and L5–S1). It is usually mild and may cause no symptoms at all. When there is pain, the first treatment is usually non-surgical care and exercises that strengthen the trunk; surgery comes into question for advanced slips or for nerve symptoms that do not settle.

tur55-43: A shoulder dislocation is when the head of the upper arm bone comes out of its socket in the shoulder; it usually happens in a fall or during sport, and most often the shoulder comes out forwards. Once a shoulder has dislocated, it may tend to dislocate again or slip partly out of place; this is called shoulder instability. Exercises done after the shoulder has been put back in place are the basis for regaining the shoulder's strength and movement.
tur55-46: After the shoulder is put back
tur55-47: Do not try to put the shoulder back in yourself; go to the emergency department as soon as possible. Do not drive; call 112 if needed.
tur55-48: The dislocation is usually confirmed with an X-ray, and the physician puts the shoulder back in place under local anaesthetic or a sedative. A sling is then given. Most people recover in 6–12 weeks; for some people recovery can take longer.
tur55-50: Take care over 40: rotator cuff tears
tur55-51: According to an article published in the BMJ, rotator cuff tears are common after a shoulder dislocation over the age of 40: in studies, a tear was found in about half of people in this age group who had a dislocation. The tear can be missed even if the X-ray taken after the shoulder is put back is normal. For this reason, the article recommends urgent ultrasound or MRI after every dislocation over the age of 40. If you cannot lift your arm after a dislocation, or weakness persists, see your physician without delay.

tur55-81: It can. In a pooled analysis of studies, about 39% of first-time anterior dislocations were followed by another dislocation or partial slipping. Being aged 40 or under, being male and having very loose joints (hyperlaxity) increase this likelihood. Physiotherapy strengthens the shoulder muscles; in young people and in recurrent dislocations, surgery may also be discussed. In a 2018 analysis pooling 22 randomised trials, about 47% of people managed without surgery after a first dislocation had no further dislocation within 2 years. Holding the arm in a special sling in external rotation did not reduce re-dislocation; the authors consider an ordinary arm sling sufficient for comfort. Because the studies differ in their patient groups, follow-up times and definitions of re-dislocation, these figures cannot be compared directly.
tur55-82: Is surgery needed after a first dislocation?
tur55-83: Not always. In a network meta-analysis pooling 22 randomised trials (BJSM, 2018), the shoulder did not dislocate again in about half of patients managed with physiotherapy after a first dislocation. Surgical repair of the joint lip (labrum), on the other hand, reduced the risk of dislocating again (moderate-quality evidence). The decision is therefore made according to age, sport, risk of re-dislocation and the person's preference; in young people and in recurrent dislocations, a shoulder specialist's opinion can be sought.
